skill.name: rust-testing
skill.description: Rust testing patterns including unit tests, integration tests, async testing, property-based testing, mocking, and coverage. Follows TDD methodology. Use when writing Rust tests — unit, integration, async, property-based, or coverage.
skill.summary: Write Rust tests with Cargo, Tokio, proptest, and mockall, then measure coverage with cargo-llvm-cov.
skill.author: affaan-m

security_audit.summary: All 64 static alerts are false positives in context, including Markdown formatting, a mock predicate, and test examples. remediation.suggestion: Pin each action to a reviewed full commit SHA. Keep the release name in a comment and review updates before repinning.

content.value_statement: Rust projects need tests that check errors, async behavior, and public interfaces. This skill shows how to write those tests, isolate dependencies, and measure coverage with Cargo tools.
actual_capabilities: Shows how to write a failing unit test, implement the required behavior, and refactor while tests pass.
Explains how to assert specific errors and organize integration tests around public APIs.
Shows Tokio test patterns for async success and timeout handling.
Demonstrates rstest cases and fixtures, proptest input strategies, and mockall trait expectations.
Shows how to write Rust doctests and configure Criterion benchmarks.
Documents Cargo test filters, coverage reports, and line coverage thresholds for CI.
limitations: Provides examples, not a runnable Rust project or an installed test runner.
Some examples reference application types or helpers that you must provide.
Tokio, rstest, proptest, mockall, and Criterion examples require suitable project dependencies.
Coverage measures which lines ran, not whether every important behavior was verified.

use_cases.title: Add Tests to a Rust Library
use_cases.description: Check valid inputs and specific error variants before changing a public function.

use_cases.title: Verify Async Service Behavior
use_cases.description: Test a successful service response and a timeout using controlled inputs instead of a live service.

use_cases.title: Track Coverage in CI
use_cases.description: Generate a coverage report and set a line coverage threshold for a Rust build.

prompt_templates.title: Write a First Unit Test
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: test one function with the standard Rust test harness.
prompt_templates.prompt: Write unit tests for this Rust function in its existing module. Cover one valid input and one error case without adding dependencies.

prompt_templates.title: Add Parameterized Cases
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: replace repeated tests with named input cases.
prompt_templates.prompt: Consolidate these repeated tests into rstest cases. Include an empty input and keep the expected result visible for each case.

prompt_templates.title: Test an Async Timeout
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: verify async behavior without waiting on a real service.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use Tokio tests to cover success and timeout paths for this async function. Use a controllable test dependency and avoid fixed sleeps.

prompt_templates.title: Combine Property Tests and Coverage
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: expand coverage of a crate with generated inputs.
prompt_templates.prompt: Add proptest round-trip tests for this encoder and decoder, using a strategy for valid inputs. Suggest a cargo-llvm-cov check and identify error cases that still need direct tests.

output_examples.input: What should I test for a configuration parser?
output: A valid configuration returns the expected port.
Malformed input returns the parsing error variant.
Keep both cases in the parser's unit tests, and add a doctest for the public example.

output_examples.input: How should I check a repository-backed service?
output: Use a trait mock to check that the service looks up the requested user ID once.
Verify that the service returns the expected user when the record exists.
Use a separate test to confirm that a missing record returns no user.

output_examples.input: What properties should I test for sorting?
output: Generate integer lists of different lengths, including empty lists.
Check that sorting preserves the original length.
Check that each adjacent pair is in nondecreasing order.

best_practices: Write a test first and verify that it fails for the expected reason.
Name each test for the behavior it verifies and assert the specific error when possible.
Use mocks to isolate dependencies and integration tests to verify behavior through public interfaces.
anti_patterns: Using fixed sleeps to wait for async work.
Sharing mutable state across tests or relying on test order.
Expecting a panic when the API already reports failure as a Result.

faq.question: Do I need extra crates for basic unit tests?
faq.answer: No. Rust provides test attributes and assertions, and Cargo runs the tests.

faq.question: How do unit tests differ from integration tests?
faq.answer: Unit tests can live next to the implementation. Integration tests live under the crate's tests directory and exercise its public API.

faq.question: Can I test an async timeout without fixed sleeps?
faq.answer: Yes. Use Tokio's paused time or coordinate the test with channels or barriers.

faq.question: When should I use proptest instead of rstest?
faq.answer: Use proptest to check a rule across generated inputs. Use rstest when you have specific cases and known expected results.

faq.question: Does this skill install coverage tools?
faq.answer: No. It shows how to use cargo-llvm-cov, which must be available in your local or CI environment.

faq.question: Can I use the CI example as written?
faq.answer: Adapt it to your repository and pin each GitHub Action to a reviewed full commit SHA before using it.
